q: Which statement describes a list in the chapter?
options: An ordered sequence of values in square brackets, whose items may be of different types
A set of unique values with no order
A fixed pair of two values
why: A list is a value that contains multiple values in an ordered sequence, and its items can be of any type.

q: A variable spam is assigned ['cat', 'bat']. How many values is spam assigned?
options: Two: one for each item of the list
One: the list value, which itself contains two items
None: a list cannot be assigned to a variable
Three: the list and its two items
why: The variable is assigned only one value, the list, although the list contains other values.

q: List: what does this program print?
why: The list has five items of five different types, and len counts the items.

q: What distinguishes [] from the string ''?
options: [] holds one item, the empty string
[] raises an error when it is printed
[] is an empty list and '' is an empty string; each contains no values of its own kind
why: The chapter says [] is an empty list that contains no values, similar to the empty string.

q: List length: what does this program print?
why: len counts the items of the outer list only, and the outer list holds two lists.

q: A list has 4 items. Which is its last valid index?
why: Counting starts at 0, so the last index is the length minus one.

q: Which three ways of naming a position in a list does the chapter teach?
options: An index from the front, a negative index from the back, and two indexes for a list of lists
A key, a value and a pair
A start, a stop and a step only
A name, a type and a size
why: The group covers the index, the negative index and the list of lists; slices are in the next group.

q: Index: what does this program print?
why: The first index is 0, so index 3 is the fourth item.

q: Why does ['cat', 'bat'][2] raise an IndexError?
options: The list has two items, so the valid indexes are 0 and 1
An index must be a negative number
A list of strings cannot be indexed
why: The last valid index is the length minus one.

q: Negative index: what does this program print?
why: Index -1 is the last item, -2 the one before it, and -3 is 'bat'.

q: For a list of four items, which negative index is the first one outside the list?
why: Valid negative indexes run from -1 to -4, and -5 raises an IndexError.

q: List of lists: what does this program print?
why: spam[1] is the inner list of numbers and its index 4 is the fifth item.

q: In spam[0][1], what does the first index choose?
options: Which item inside the inner list
why: The first index dictates which list value to use, and the second indicates the value within that list.

q: What does a slice of a list give back?
options: The selected items as separate values
A string made of the items
A new list holding the selected items
The same list, changed in place
why: A slice takes several items from a list in one expression and gives them back as a new list.

q: Slice: what does this program print?
why: A slice starts at the first index and goes up to, but does not include, the second.

q: How many items does spam[2:7] have when spam holds ten items?
why: The length of the slice is the end minus the start.

q: Omitted slice ends: what does this program print?
why: Leaving out the first index means 0 and leaving out the second means the length; the two slices meet without a gap.

q: Which expression makes a copy of the list spam?
why: A slice with both numbers left out takes every item and gives a new list.

q: Slice step: what does this program print?
why: A step of 2 takes every second item and a step of -1 reverses the order.

q: Which step value raises a ValueError in a slice?
why: The slice step cannot be zero.

q: Which operations does the branch on changing a list cover?
why: The branch covers replacement by assignment, adding, removing and combining lists.

q: When an item of a list is replaced by assignment to its index, what changes?
options: A new list is made and the name moves to it
Only the name used in the assignment sees the change
Nothing, until the list is printed
The list changes in place; every name that refers to it sees the new item
why: Replacement changes the list and not the variable.

q: Item assignment: what does this program print?
code:
spam = ['cat', 'bat', 'rat', 'elephant']
spam[1] = 'aardvark'
spam[2] = spam[1]
spam[-1] = 12345
print(spam)
why: Each assignment replaces one item in place, and the third copies the value of the item at index 1.

q: What does spam[5] = 'x' do when spam has three items?
options: Adds 'x' at index 5 and fills the gap with None
Raises an IndexError, because assignment cannot create a new place
why: Assignment to an index replaces an existing item; use append or insert to add.

q: Which three methods add items to a list?
why: The group explains the three ways to add items.

q: append: what does this program print?
why: append changes the list in place and returns None, so the first line printed is None.

q: Why is spam = spam.append('moose') a mistake?
options: append returns a new list that must be sorted first
append returns None, so the name would be bound to None and the list lost
why: The return value of append is None, and it modifies the list in place.

q: insert: what does this program print?
why: insert puts the value at the given index and moves the later items one place along.

q: What happens with spam.insert(100, 'x') on a list of three items?
options: The value is added at the front
The value is added at the end
why: An index beyond the end places the item at the end.

q: extend: what does this program print?
code:
a = [1, 2, 3]
a.extend(['A', 'B'])
b = [1, 2, 3]
b.append(['A', 'B'])
print(len(a), len(b))
why: extend adds every item of its argument, while append adds the argument as one item.

q: What does [1, 2, 3].extend('ab') produce in the list?
options: [1, 2, 3, 'a', 'b'], because the string is an iterable of characters
why: extend takes every item of an iterable, and a string yields its characters.

q: Which three operations remove items from a list?
why: The group explains del, remove and pop.

q: del statement: what does this program print?
why: del removes the item at the index and the later items move down.

q: When is del the right choice to remove an item?
options: When only the value of the item is known
When the index of the item is known
When the removed item is needed afterwards
why: del is useful when you know the index, remove when you know the value.

q: remove: what does this program print?
why: remove deletes only the first item equal to the value.

q: What does ['a'].remove('b') do?
options: Returns None and leaves the list as it is
Raises a ValueError, because the value is not in the list
why: remove raises a ValueError when the value is absent.

q: pop: what does this program print?
why: pop removes and returns the last item by default and the item at the index when one is given.

q: What does [].pop() do?
options: Raises an IndexError, because there is no item to remove
why: pop on an empty list raises an IndexError.

q: Which operators combine lists?
options: + joins two lists and * repeats a list
why: The operators of strings also work on lists.

q: List concatenation: what does this program print?
why: The + operator builds a new list and leaves both operands unchanged.

q: What does [1, 2] + 3 do?
options: Raises a TypeError, because both operands must be lists
why: A list can be concatenated only with another list.

q: List replication: what does this program print?
why: The * operator repeats the items, and an empty list repeated is still empty.

q: Why is [0] * 70 a safe way to make 70 counters?
options: Integers are lists of one item
The items are integers, which cannot be changed through a shared reference
why: Replication repeats references, and an immutable item cannot be changed.

q: Augmented assignment: what does this program print?
code:
bacon = ['Zophie']
bacon *= 3
spam = 'Hello,'
spam += ' world!'
print(bacon, spam)
why: bacon *= 3 means bacon = bacon * 3, and += joins the strings.

q: For a list x, how does x += [1] differ from x = x + [1] when another name y refers to the same list?
options: x = x + [1] changes the shared list, x += [1] does not
x += [1] changes the shared list, so y sees it; x = x + [1] makes a new list that y does not see
why: Augmented assignment on a list extends it in place, while + builds a new list.

q: What are the two services that this branch offers for a list?
options: Asking where a value is and putting the items in order
why: Searching and ordering are the two services asked of a collection more than any other.

q: What is a method, in the chapter's words?
options: A variable that holds a function
A function that is called on a value
why: A method is the same thing as a function, except it is called on a value.

q: Method: what does this program print?
why: append belongs to lists, so the string has no such attribute.

q: Why does spam.append (without parentheses) append nothing?
options: It names the bound method but does not call it
why: A call needs parentheses.

q: What does in answer, and what does index answer?
options: in answers with a position, index with yes or no
in answers yes or no, index answers with a position
why: The operator tests for presence and the method returns the position.

q: in and not in operators: what does this program print?
code:
spam = ['hello', 'hi', 'howdy', 'heyas']
print('howdy' in spam, 'cat' in spam, 'cat' not in spam)
why: in tests whether an item equals the value, and not in gives the opposite.

q: What is the difference between 'ab' in 'cabd' and 'ab' in ['cabd']?
options: The first is False and the second is True
The first tests for a substring and is True; the second tests for an item equal to 'ab' and is False
why: On a string in tests for a substring; on a list it tests for an equal item.

q: index method: what does this program print?
why: index returns the position of the first match.

q: What does spam.index('x') do when 'x' is not in spam?
options: Returns the length of the list
why: index raises an error rather than returning a value that could be mistaken for an index.

q: Short-circuiting: what does this program print?
why: len(spam) > 0 is False, so Python does not evaluate spam[0].

q: Why does spam[0] == 'cat' and len(spam) > 0 still fail on an empty list?
options: and evaluates the right operand first
The guard must come first: the left operand is evaluated before the right
len cannot be used with and
== has no meaning for an empty list
why: Short-circuiting only helps when the test is on the left.

q: What design rule do sort and sorted show?
options: A method that changes a list in place returns None; a function that makes a new list returns it
Both change the list in place
why: The group contrasts the in-place method with the function that returns a new list.

q: sort method: what does this program print?
why: sort returns None, so the assignment replaces the list with None.

q: Why does ['Alice', 'ants', 'Bob'].sort() put 'ants' last?
options: Python sorts by the length of the string
Python sorts in reverse by default
Strings are ordered by character code and capital letters come before lowercase ones
why: The chapter calls this ASCIIbetical order.

q: key and reverse arguments: what does this program print?
why: The key makes the comparison treat every item as lowercase; equal keys keep their original order.

q: What must be passed as the key argument?
options: A function, written without parentheses, such as str.lower
why: key names the function itself, which is applied to each item before the comparison.

q: reverse method: what does this program print?
why: reverse changes the list in place and returns None.

q: Which expression gives a reversed copy and leaves the list unchanged?
why: A slice with step -1 is a new list in reverse order.

q: sorted function: what does this program print?
why: sorted returns a new ordered list and leaves the original alone.

q: What type is the result of sorted('banana')?
why: sorted always returns a list.

q: What does this branch say a for loop over a list does?
options: It repeats its block once for each character
It repeats its block once for each item of the list
It repeats its block until the list is empty
why: Technically, a for loop repeats its block once for each item in a list value.

q: Which four forms of looping does the group compare?
options: The loop over indexes, enumerate, the loop that must not change its list, and the list comprehension
why: The group explains the four forms that matter in practice.

q: Loop over the indexes: what does this program print?
code:
supplies = ['pens', 'staplers', 'binders']
print([i for i in range(len(supplies))])
why: range(len(supplies)) yields every index from 0 to the length minus one.

q: Why does for i in range(len(spam) + 1): print(spam[i]) fail?
options: range does not accept a sum
The last value of i is len(spam), which is outside the list
why: The loop reaches one place too far and raises an IndexError at the last pass.

q: enumerate function: what does this program print?
why: enumerate yields pairs of the count and the item, and start sets the first count.

q: In for index, item in enumerate(supplies), which comes first?
why: enumerate returns the index and then the item.

q: Changing a list during a loop: what does this program print?
code:
items = ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd']
for x in items:
    items.remove(x)
print(items)
why: Each removal moves later items under the loop's position, so every second item is skipped.

q: Which remedy avoids the problem of removing items during a loop?
options: Loop over the same list but call sort first
Build a new list with a comprehension, or loop over a copy
Use a while loop over the same list without any change
Remove items from the end only with remove
why: The documentation advises looping over a copy or creating a new collection.

q: List comprehension: what does this program print?
code: print([x * x for x in range(6) if x % 2 == 0])
why: The if clause keeps the even numbers 0, 2 and 4, and the expression squares them.

q: Does a list comprehension change the list it reads?
options: Yes, it changes the list in place
Only when it has an if clause
Only when the variable is reused
No, it builds a new list
why: A comprehension evaluates its expression for each item and appends the result to a new list.

q: What does unpacking do?
options: Removes the items from the list
Sorts the items into variables by name
Assigns the items of a list to several variables in one statement
Copies the list into one variable
why: Unpacking is the multiple assignment trick and its starred form.

q: Multiple assignment trick: what does this program print?
code:
cat = ['fat', 'gray', 'loud']
size, color, disposition = cat
print(color)
why: The names take the items from left to right.

q: What happens with a, b = [1, 2, 3]?
options: a and b get 1 and 2 and the 3 is dropped
A ValueError, because there are more items than names
why: The number of variables and the length of the list must be exactly equal.

q: Starred unpacking: what does this program print?
why: The starred name collects the leftover items as a list.

q: What does the starred name receive in a, *m, z = [1, 2]?
why: Two items fill a and z, and nothing is left for the starred name.

q: What is the chapter's summary of how variables hold lists?
options: A variable holds a reference to the list, not the list itself
A variable holds a copy of the list
A variable holds the length of the list
A variable holds the first item of the list
why: Variables never contain values; they contain references to values.

q: Which are the sequence data types the chapter names?
options: Lists, strings, range objects and tuples
why: The Python sequence data types include lists, strings, range objects and tuples.

q: Strings and ranges as sequences: what does this program print?
code:
name = 'Zophie'
print(name[0], name[-2], name[0:4], 'Zo' in name)
why: A string is indexed, sliced and searched like a list of characters.

q: Which operations work on strings the same way as on lists?
options: Indexing, slicing, for loops, len and in
why: The sequence operations are shared; the changing methods are not.

q: Mutable and immutable values: what does this program print?
options: 'str' object does not support item assignment
'tuple' object does not support item assignment
why: A string is immutable, so assignment to one of its characters raises a TypeError.

q: After eggs = ['A', 'B', 'C'] and eggs = ['x', 'y', 'z'], what happened to the first list?
options: It was copied into the new list
It was not modified; a new list replaced it under the name eggs
why: Reassigning the name binds it to a new list; changing in place needs del and append.

q: Tuple: what does this program print?
why: A tuple of one value needs the trailing comma; without it the parentheses only group.

q: What is the main difference between a tuple and a list?
options: A tuple is written with square brackets
A tuple cannot be changed after it is made
A tuple can hold only numbers
why: Tuples, like strings, are immutable.

q: What is the chapter's better metaphor for a variable than a box?
options: A drawer that holds a copy of the value
A paper name tag attached to a value with string
A label painted on the value
A number that counts the uses of the value
why: Variables are paper name tags attached to values.

q: Aliasing: what does this program print?
why: eggs = spam copies only the reference, so both names refer to one list.

q: After spam = 42, eggs = spam and spam = 99, what is eggs?
why: The reassignment attaches the name spam to a new value; eggs still refers to 42.

q: Lists as function arguments: what does this program print?
code:
def eggs(some_parameter):
    some_parameter.append('Hello')

spam = [1, 2, 3]
eggs(spam)
print(spam)
why: The parameter refers to the caller's list, so the append changes it.

q: A function does p = p + ['x'] on its list parameter p. What does the caller's list show?
options: The new item, because lists are passed by reference
No change, because + built a new list and only the parameter's name moved to it
why: Assignment to the parameter does not affect the caller's name.

q: Repeating a list of lists: what does this program print?
why: The two rows are one inner list referred to twice.

q: How can a grid of independent rows be built?
options: With a comprehension: [[0] * 3 for _ in range(2)]
With copy.copy on the first row only
why: The comprehension evaluates [0] * 3 once for every row.

q: Which module provides copy.copy and copy.deepcopy?
why: Python provides a module named copy for the purpose.

q: Shallow copy: what does this program print?
code:
import copy
spam = ['A', 'B', 'C']
cheese = copy.copy(spam)
cheese[1] = 42
print(spam, cheese)
why: The copy is a separate list, so replacing one of its items does not reach the original.

q: After c = copy.copy([[1], [2]]) and c[0].append(9), what is the original list?
options: [[1, 9], [2]], because the inner list is shared
why: A shallow copy shares the objects it holds.

q: Deep copy: what does this program print?
code:
import copy
spam = [[1], [2]]
c = copy.deepcopy(spam)
c[0].append(9)
print(spam, c)
why: The deep copy copies the inner lists, so nothing is shared.

q: When is copy.deepcopy needed?
options: When the list holds only numbers
When the list contains lists or dictionaries that the program will change
why: The shallow copy is enough for immutable items.

q: What do the four programs of the chapter have in common?
options: Each is built around a list
why: The programs are the test of the chapter: each uses list operations for a purpose.

q: Which two functions of the random module take a list in the chapter?
why: The group explains random.choice and random.shuffle.

q: Which statement about this program is true?
code:
import random
pets = ['Dog', 'Cat', 'Moose']
print(random.choice(pets) in pets, len(pets))
why: choice returns an item of the list and does not change the list.

q: What does random.choice([]) raise?
why: There is nothing to choose from in an empty sequence.

q: random.shuffle: what does this program print?
why: shuffle reorders the list in place and returns None; sorting shows the same four items.

q: Why does random.shuffle(('a', 'b')) raise a TypeError?
options: A tuple cannot be changed in place
why: shuffle modifies the list in place and so needs a mutable sequence.

q: What do the programs of the group show about checking edge cases?
options: Only the Magic 8 Ball has edge cases
They should be tested on the empty list and the one-item list
why: Each program is a model for the habit of testing small lists.

q: Magic 8 Ball with a list: what does this program print?
code:
messages = ['It is certain', 'It is decidedly so', 'Yes definitely']
print(len(messages) - 1)
why: The largest index of a list of three items is 2, the upper bound for randint.

q: What is the benefit of putting the answers in a list?
options: Answers can be added or removed without changing other lines
why: The chapter says to change fewer lines when strings are added and removed.

q: Matrix screensaver: what does this program print?
code:
WIDTH = 70
columns = [0] * WIDTH
columns[3] = 5
columns[3] -= 1
print(len(columns), columns[3], columns[4])
why: The list has one counter per column; the counter at index 3 counted down once.

q: In the screensaver, what does a counter above zero mean?
options: A stream of digits is running in that column
The program is about to stop
The column has been printed twice
why: A counter above zero prints a random 0 or 1 and counts down.

q: Comma Code: what does this program print?
why: All items but the last are joined with a comma and a space, then ', and ' and the last item are added.

q: Which edge case does the chapter ask to test for Comma Code?
options: A list of one hundred items
why: items[-1] on an empty list would raise an IndexError.

q: Coin Flip Streaks: what does this program print?
code:
flips = ['H', 'T', 'T', 'T', 'T', 'T', 'T', 'H']
print([flips[i:i + 6] == ['T'] * 6 for i in range(len(flips) - 5)])
why: Three windows of six items exist in a list of eight, and only the middle one is all T.

q: Why does the program count an experiment once even if it has several streaks?
options: It removes the streak from the list
It breaks out of the search at the first streak
why: Counting once is what the break does.

q: List length: what does this second program print?
why: len is evaluated after the append, so the list has three items.

q: Index: what does this second program print?
why: The last index len(spam) - 1 and the index -1 name the same item.

q: Slice: what does this second program print?
why: A slice never raises an error for an end that is too far, and a start after the end gives an empty list.

q: in and not in operators: what does this second program print?
why: 1 == 1.0, a substring test succeeds, and 'ab' is not an item of the list.

q: sort method: what does this second program print?
why: Python cannot compare a number with a string.

q: pop: what does this second program print?
why: pop on an empty list raises an IndexError with its own message.

q: index method: what does this second program print?
why: The search starts at position 1 and finds the second 'a'.

q: Aliasing: what does this second program print?
code:
spam = [1]
eggs = spam
spam = spam + [2]
print(eggs)
why: spam + [2] builds a new list, so eggs still refers to the old one.
